title: Iran Says It Can Reopen a Key Oil Waterway in Just 7 Days
summary:
Imagine a giant doorway in the ocean where about 18 ships squeeze through every day. That's the Strait of Hormuz. Right now, Iran is blocking it — and that's a big deal for oil and trade around the world.

On Friday, Iran's Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, said his country has a deal for the US. If the US meets certain conditions, the strait could reopen in seven days. "The choice now rests with the United States," he said.

Araghchi said the conditions are already written in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) — a signed agreement — from June 18. That 14-point plan said Iran would never build a nuclear weapon, the US would end its naval blockade, and both sides would stop fighting.

But the deal fell apart. The US and Israel launched airstrikes on Iran on February 28. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases, and by blocking the strait. Since then, ships have been attacked if Iran says they don't have permission to pass.

Iran's President, Masoud Pezeshkian, also said Iran would let UN nuclear inspectors back in. He denied that Iran is trying to build a nuclear bomb.

Trump is reportedly skeptical. He has told staff he thinks more bombing is likely. Meanwhile, Yemen's Houthis — allies of Iran — are attacking oil exports in the Red Sea. So even if the Strait of Hormuz reopens, the waters around the Middle East are still risky.
why_it_matters: Oil travels by ship through this narrow doorway, so when it is blocked, prices for things like gas can go up — something families notice at the pump.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow stretch of water that connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean, and a very large share of the world's oil travels through it on ships.

Iran is a country in the Middle East; the United Nations (a group where almost all countries meet to talk about big world problems) sends inspectors to check that countries are not building nuclear bombs.
Yemen's Houthis are a group that controls part of Yemen, a country south of Saudi Arabia, and they have fought with help from Iran.
Article_Structure: WHO: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, President Donald Trump, and Yemen's Houthis.
WHAT: Iran says it can reopen the blocked Strait of Hormuz in seven days if the United States meets the conditions in a signed June 18 agreement.
WHERE: The Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East, plus the Red Sea near Yemen.
WHY: The strait is a narrow doorway that about 18 ships use every day, so blocking it affects oil and trade all around the world.
